JACKSON — On Earth Day, Mississippi leaders and conservation advocates are encouraging residents to step outside and explore the landscapes that have long defined the state’s identity.

From winding rivers and cypress-filled bayous to pine forests and rolling hills, Mississippi’s outdoors tell a story of ecosystems that have shaped communities and sustained generations. The Great Mississippi Nature Trail brings many of those landscapes together, offering access to natural areas, state parks, wildlife refuges and scenic trails across the state.

The trail connects destinations ranging from waterfalls and rail trails to quiet wilderness areas, showcasing Mississippi’s ecological diversity and cultural history.

“Happy Earth Day,” the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce posted on Facebook Wednesday. “There’s no better time to celebrate Native Plant Month than by getting outside and discovering the beauty of Mississippi’s natural landscape.”

When most people think of Mississippi, they picture the Delta, the blues, or the Mississippi River itself. But tucked along the Great Mississippi Nature Trail is a botanical world full of carnivorous plants, ancient cypress groves, and some of the most diverse native flora in the entire country.

If you’re interested in a starting point, go with Crosby Arboretum in Picayune. This 104-acre native plant conservatory is home to more than 700 species of trees, shrubs, wildflowers, and grasses, and that’s just the interpretive center. Wander into the pitcher plant bogs and you’ll find yourself face to face with some of nature’s most clever survivors. Sundews have a sticky “dew” designed to trap unsuspecting insects. Parrot pitcher plants, which are compact little carnivorous plants only four to six inches tall, sit quietly waiting for their next meal.

Head north and watch the landscape shift noticeably. At Leroy Percy State Park, huge oaks draped in Spanish moss frame artesian springs that have been flowing for centuries. At Tishomingo State Park, swamp cypress trees line Bear Creek against a backdrop of sandstone bluffs.

In the Delta, the Yazoo National Wildlife Refuge and Delta National Forest tell a different story: one of bottomland hardwoods, where oak, ash, elm, and cottonwood form a canopy that supports white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and hundreds of migratory bird species.

What ties all of these places together is Mississippi’s extensive plant diversity. The state is home to roughly 200 native tree species alone, from longleaf pine in the piney woods of the south to hardwood forests in the north. Some of the rarest plants in the country — bog flax, bog spicebush, and native orchids — cling to existence in the Gulf Coast’s wet pine savannas, where less than 3% of the original habitat remains.

The Great Mississippi Nature Trail is a chance to see the state’s wild side before it disappears. Officials said the trail provides opportunities for all types of visitors, whether they are planning a family outing, a scenic drive or a weekend on the water.

Popular stops along the route include state parks such as LeFleur’s Bluff State Park, Tishomingo State Park and Percy Quin State Park, as well as federal sites like the Natchez Trace Parkway and the Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge. Local favorites such as the Longleaf Trace and unique natural landmarks like Red Bluff also draw visitors each year.

Advocates say spending time outdoors is not only a way to celebrate Earth Day, but also a way to build a deeper connection to the environment.

The Department of Agriculture and Commerce encouraged Mississippians to explore areas where native plants thrive, noting that understanding local ecosystems can help residents make more sustainable choices at home.

For those planning a trip, officials recommend bringing plenty of water, checking trail conditions ahead of time and following “Leave No Trace” principles to protect natural resources. Spring and fall are often considered the best times to visit, offering milder weather and increased wildlife activity. Activities along the trail range from hiking and fishing to kayaking and wildlife viewing, with many sites designed to accommodate families through accessible boardwalks and rail trails.

As Earth Day underscores the importance of conservation, leaders say Mississippi’s natural spaces remain both a resource and a responsibility.

By exploring the state’s outdoors, they say, residents can better appreciate the landscapes that make Mississippi unique and help ensure they are preserved for future generations.
https://darkhorsepressnow.com/news/2026-.summary: JACKSON — On Earth Day, Mississippi leaders and conservation advocates are encouraging residents to step outside and explore the landscapes that have long defined the state’s identity.

GULFPORT — A Florida woman was arrested after deputies seized 6.6 pounds of cocaine during a traffic stop on Interstate 10 in Gulfport, authorities said.

Harrison County Sheriff Matt Haley announced Thursday that the drugs were recovered April 22 during a stop at about 1:33 p.m. on eastbound I-10 near the 36-mile marker.

A deputy with the Harrison County Sheriff’s Office Criminal Interdiction Division stopped a Nissan Altima and made contact with the driver, identified as Amy Broadt of Fort Walton Beach, Florida. During the stop, a K-9 alerted to the presence of narcotics in the vehicle, officials said.

Deputies conducted a probable cause search and found approximately 6.6 pounds of cocaine inside a bag in the trunk, according to the sheriff’s office.

Harrison County narcotics investigators responded to the scene and took over the case.

Broadt was booked into the Harrison County jail and charged with aggravated trafficking of cocaine. Her bond was set at $250,000 by Judge Albert Fountain.

No additional information was immediately released.

CARROLL COUNTY — A routine traffic stop in Carroll County led to the arrest of a 28-year-old man on multiple charges, including DUI, drug possession and weapons violations, authorities said.

Carroll County deputies stopped a vehicle Sunday, April 19, on Highway 7. During the investigation, deputies took Dallas Purifoy into custody and transported him to the Carroll County Regional Correctional Facility.

Purifoy was charged with DUI — other, possession of controlled substances, including marijuana and ecstasy pills, firearm enhancement and concealment of weapons. He was later released on a $40,000 bond.

Sheriff Clint Walker said the arrest highlights the importance of proactive enforcement.

“Our deputies are well trained at spotting signs of impaired driving,” Walker said. “These stops are made to protect the public as they go about their business driving on the roads and highways of our county.”

Walker said the deputies’ investigation led to the discovery and seizure of both drugs and weapons.

“It is well known that illegal drugs fuel the epidemic of gun violence in our country,” he said. “Carroll County will not tolerate it in any shape, form or fashion. The safety and security of the people of our county is too important.”

No additional details were immediately released.

No explosives or injuries were immediately reported.

The Laurel Police Department is continuing to investigate the source of the threats. Officials said the sheriff’s department remains ready to assist as needed.

UPDATE: A third person has been arrested in the March 30th double homicide of Terry Burrell Jr. and Khloe “Chloe” Hudson. Milisen Martinez (21) is charged with Accessory After the Fact of Murder.

HINDS COUNTY – Two young men have been arrested and charged with capital murder in the killings of two 16-year-old Lanier High School students whose bodies were found last month in rural Hinds County, authorities said.

Bruce White, 18, and Ezra White, 19, were taken into custody Wednesday evening following weeks of investigation into the deaths of Terrell Burrell Jr. and Khloe Hudson, according to Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones. Both suspects are being held at the Raymond Detention Center pending an initial court appearance, which could come as early as Monday.

Jones said investigators developed enough evidence to elevate the charges beyond murder.

“We do have enough evidence … to say that they’re both being charged with not just murder, but both are being charged with capital murder due to some of the circumstances that we’ve been able to discover during the course of the investigation,” Jones said during a Thursday press conference.

Burrell and Hudson were reported missing to the Jackson Police Department before their bodies were discovered March 30 along South Springdale Road in the Pocahontas community. Jones said early findings indicated the killings were not random and that the victims knew each other.

Investigators also believe the victims and suspects were acquainted prior to the killings.

“There is an indication there is a victim-to-offender knowledge, meaning they did know each other prior to this incident,” Jones said. “We do believe that they were both targeted.”

Authorities have not publicly identified a specific motive, but Jones said the case reflects ongoing concerns about youth violence and access to firearms.

“We’re talking about two 16-year-olds that lost their life … and now you’re having families facing an 18-year-old and a 19-year-old being allegedly involved,” he said. “This is something that we stress: youth violence, youth with guns, being reckless, irresponsible with guns.”

Jones said at least one of the suspects may have ties to the rural area where the bodies were found, and investigators believe the killings likely occurred at or near that location, though additional crime scenes have not been ruled out.

The sheriff also warned that additional arrests or charges are possible as the investigation continues.

“There’s a strong possibility there could be further arrests and or charges,” Jones said. “We continue to follow leads, gather evidence and conduct interviews to ensure every responsible party is held fully accountable.”

Jones credited multiple agencies for their role in the investigation, including the Jackson Police Department and Capitol Police, saying early information from Jackson investigators helped identify the suspects within days of the killings.

“Our thoughts remain with the families, classmates and community members grieving this heartbreaking loss,” Jones said. “We remain committed to transparency, diligence and justice.”

Anyone with additional information is urged to contact the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office or Crime Stoppers.

Therese Apel contributed to this report.

Authorities identified those arrested as Cassandra McCaplin, Ti’Caryunia McCaplin, Shanutavia Mack and Edricka Brown.

All four made their initial appearances before Judge David Flowers, who set bond at $500 cash for each defendant, according to the sheriff’s office.

The sheriff’s office said the investigation remains ongoing and that warrants have been issued for additional people connected to the incident. Authorities said charges in the case range from simple assault to disturbing the peace.

The sheriff’s office is urging anyone seen in the video, whether actively involved in the fight or present during the altercation, to turn themselves in. Authorities said even people who considered themselves spectators could face charges depending on their level of involvement.

Sheriff Edward Goods said the department remains committed to maintaining order and holding people accountable for actions that threaten public safety.

Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Claiborne County Sheriff’s Office.

COLUMBUS- A fugitive wanted on multiple charges was arrested Thursday evening after a short standoff at an apartment in East Columbus, according to the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office.

Authorities said 35-year-old Justin Contrell Hairston was taken into custody at about 6 p.m. April 23.

The sheriff’s office said Hairston was wanted on a bench warrant charging him with trafficking cocaine, possession of a firearm by a felon and simple assault on a corrections officer. Authorities said he is also being charged as a habitual offender.

According to the sheriff’s office, U.S. Marshals and Lowndes County deputies responded to the apartment and made contact with Hairston, ordering him multiple times to come out.

When Hairston refused to comply, a team of U.S. Marshals entered the apartment, authorities said. After he continued refusing lawful commands, Hairston was tased and taken into custody without further incident.

He was transported to the Lowndes County Adult Detention Center, where he is being held without bond, according to the sheriff’s office.

Sheriff Eddie Hawkins praised the cooperation between his department and the U.S. Marshals Service, saying the arrest showed the value of interagency teamwork in locating fugitives and protecting the community.

The case remains under investigation.

GEORGE COUNTY – The George County Sheriff’s Office announced multiple arrests Friday following separate investigations involving serious criminal allegations.

The sheriff’s office said the cases are the result of extended investigations by its Criminal Investigations Division.

Johny D. Broome, 40, of Lucedale, was arrested April 22 and charged with one count of sexual battery and two counts of molestation involving touching of a child for lustful purposes, according to the sheriff’s office.

Authorities said warrants were issued by George County Justice Court after what they described as a lengthy investigation. Justice Court Judge Marty Davis set Broome’s bond at $150,000 on the sexual battery charge and $25,000 on each molestation charge, for a total bond of $200,000.

In a separate case, John K. Fisher, 55, of Lucedale, turned himself in April 24 on an outstanding arrest warrant, the sheriff’s office said. Authorities said Fisher is charged with one count of molestation involving touching of a child for lustful purposes. Judge Davis set Fisher’s bond at $15,000.

The sheriff’s office also announced the arrest of Tony K. Fairley, 49, in the Silverhill community of Baldwin County, Alabama, pending extradition to George County.

Authorities said multiple people reported incidents of sexual and physical abuse over several years in George County. Following what the sheriff’s office described as an extensive investigation, warrants were issued charging Fairley with three counts of sexual battery and two counts of child abuse.

With help from the Foley Police Department and the Baldwin County Sheriff’s Office, Fairley was located and taken into custody, according to authorities. He is being held in the Baldwin County Jail while awaiting extradition to George County.

Sheriff Mitchell Mixon said the cases reflect the commitment of investigators to pursue justice and protect the community.

The investigations remain ongoing, and additional information may be released later. The sheriff’s office said all suspects are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in court.

MARION COUNTY – A Marion County man has been arrested in connection with a house fire that seriously injured two people and now faces arson and attempted murder charges, according to the Marion County Sheriff’s Office.

Authorities said deputies and fire crews responded April 19 to a reported structure fire at 172 Fleet Holmes Road. Deputies with the Marion County Sheriff’s Office and units from the Foxworth and Southwest fire departments were dispatched to the scene.

When first responders arrived, they found two occupants suffering from smoke inhalation and burn injuries, according to the sheriff’s office. AAA Ambulance Service took both victims to a local hospital. One of the victims was later airlifted to the University of Mississippi Medical Center and remains in critical condition.

Following an investigation by the Marion County Sheriff’s Office and the State Fire Marshal’s Office, investigators determined that Bryan Aubrey Turnage, the son of the victims, had allegedly made prior threats to burn the home while his parents were inside.

Authorities said Turnage was not at the scene when emergency personnel arrived.

On April 23, deputies located Turnage at a residence on John Thornhill Road, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said he tried to run but was captured after a brief foot chase and taken into custody without further incident.

Turnage was booked into the Marion County Jail and charged with one count of arson and two counts of attempted murder, authorities said.

The investigation remains ongoing.

JACKSON — The Mississippi Supreme Court has revived a defamation lawsuit filed by former Gov. Phil Bryant and his wife against Mississippi Today and several of its journalists, ruling that the case was improperly dismissed by a lower court.

In a decision issued April 23, the high court reversed a Madison County Circuit Court order that dismissed the Bryants’ claims and sent the case back for further proceedings.

The Bryants sued Mississippi Today, reporter Anna Wolfe and others, alleging defamation, false light and loss of consortium tied to reporting about the misuse of federal welfare funds. A trial judge dismissed the lawsuit in 2025, finding the complaint failed to state a claim.

However, the Supreme Court ruled that Mississippi’s notice-pleading standard requires only that a complaint present a plausible claim for relief, not prove it at the outset.

The justices found that the Bryants’ complaint sufficiently alleged defamation, including claims that statements made by the news organization were false and published with actual malice — a key legal standard for public figures.

The court noted that the complaint repeatedly asserted actual malice and included specific examples of allegedly defamatory statements. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, the court said, those allegations must be accepted as true.

Mississippi Today argued that the claims were contradicted by statements and evidence referenced in the complaint. But the Supreme Court said such factual disputes are not appropriate to resolve before trial.

“A complaint does not prove evidence,” the court wrote, adding that dismissal is only proper when there is no possible set of facts that would entitle a plaintiff to relief.

The ruling also dismissed as moot the Bryants’ appeal of an earlier denial of partial summary judgment, finding that issue was no longer relevant after the filing of an amended complaint.

The case now returns to the Madison County Circuit Court for further proceedings.

JACKSON — The Mississippi Supreme Court has upheld the first-degree murder conviction and life sentence of a Stone County man who killed and decapitated his mother, rejecting arguments that evidence was improperly obtained and that he was legally insane at the time of the crime.

In a decision issued April 23, the court affirmed the conviction of Terelle Anterion Johnson, who was found guilty by a jury after raising an insanity defense at trial.

Johnson was convicted in the 2018 killing of his mother, Sherry Johnson, at their home in Stone County. Authorities discovered her body after responding to a welfare check requested by family members who had not heard from her for several days.

According to court records, Johnson initially told relatives his mother was on vacation and refused to let them inside the home. Deputies later arrived and were allowed inside, where they began searching for her. During the search, officers found her decapitated body in the backyard and later recovered her head outside a nearby fence.

Investigators said Johnson later confessed to the killing during a recorded interview and again in a phone call from jail.

At trial, Johnson’s defense argued he suffered from severe mental illness and could not distinguish right from wrong. A defense expert testified that Johnson experienced delusions and paranoia, including a belief that his mother had been replaced by another person.

However, a state expert testified that although Johnson had a mental illness, he understood his actions and knew they were wrong at the time of the killing.

The Supreme Court ruled that the jury was entitled to weigh the conflicting testimony and that the verdict was supported by the evidence.

Justices also rejected Johnson’s claims that evidence should have been suppressed due to a warrantless search, finding that he consented to deputies entering the home and that the victim’s body would have been discovered regardless.

The court further found no reversible error in the trial judge’s decisions on jury instructions, admission of evidence, or limits placed on closing arguments.

Johnson was sentenced to life in prison, and the high court’s ruling leaves that sentence in place.

STARKVILLE — For the first time in program history, the Mississippi State University Western Equestrian Team is bound for nationals. The team is set to compete in the Intercollegiate Horse Shows Association (IHSA) National Finals held May 1-3 at Tryon International in Mill Spring, North Carolina.

Ashley Glenn, MSU Equestrian Team head coach, said while individual riders from MSU have competed at nationals in the past, this is a first for the team.

“It’s the determination of our riders that defines our team,” said Glenn, also facilities supervisor of the Mississippi Agricultural and Forestry Experiment Station’s Equine Unit. “Within IHSA, not every rider has to be an expert. We have students who’ve never had a formal lesson and others who have ridden horses their entire lives. This allows the team members to learn from one another, create a support system and build a strong bond within the team.”

Natalie Ruha, a senior criminology major from Alabaster, Alabama, has been around horses since childhood. Guided by her grandmother—a professional horse trainer—and her mother, she began showing ponies at just a few years old. When she entered college, she couldn’t imagine her life without horses, leading her to join the team where she has competed for four years and now serves as team captain.

To advance as a team, MSU needed a top four finish at the IHSA semifinals, held March 21–22 at Murray State University in Kentucky, a goal Ruha said was driven not by individual ambition, but by a shared commitment to one another.

“We delivered some of the strongest rides of our careers,” Ruha said. “We stepped up not just to qualify as a team, but to make sure our teammates had the opportunity to compete on that national stage.”

At competition, each rider begins with an unfamiliar horse, randomly assigned a steed at the venue. Students compete at different levels, from beginner to open. The events showcase the riders’ ability to navigate the horse through complex patterns and maneuvers.

The team is funded by fundraisers and donations. Those interested in supporting the team can contribute through the MSU Foundation at https://dda.msstate.edu/give-now?f=312934 .

The following students will compete: ALABASTER, Alabama—Natalie Ruha, criminology senior, High Point Rider competition, Individual Open Horsemanship, Team Open Horsemanship CLANTON, Alabama—Carrie Brigham, agricultural engineering technology and business freshman, Team Level 2 Horsemanship FILLMORE, Utah—Lillie Reid, animal and dairy sciences senior, Team Rookie Horsemanship FLORENCE—Wren Algee, psychology junior, Individual Level 2 Horsemanship MADISON, Alabama—Sarah Broyles, animal and dairy sciences junior, Team Beginner Horsemanship MADISONVILLE, Louisiana—Hayley Pettus, animal and dairy sciences junior, Individual Beginner Horsemanship MORRISTON, Florida—Breana Souders, animal and dairy sciences senior, Team Ranch Riding NASHVILLE, Tennessee—Olivia Trotter, psychology senior, Individual Rookie Horsemanship PELL CITY, Alabama—Chloe Joiner, animal and dairy sciences sophomore, Team Level 1 Horsemanship WALNUT GROVE—Makenzie Moore, veterinary medical technology junior, Team Reining

OXFORD — Two upcoming events in Oxford aim to support entrepreneurs and small business owners through training, networking and funding opportunities, local organizers announced.

Oxford-Lafayette Inc. is partnering with the Yoknapatawpha Arts Council to host a free business workshop April 28 focused on branding and effective messaging. The session will run from 6 to 8 p.m. at The Powerhouse on South 14th Street.

The workshop, part of the Big Bad Business Series, will be led by Red Window Communications and will include networking opportunities and light refreshments. Organizers said the session is designed to help business owners build consistency and strengthen their brand identity.

The series is funded in part by the National Endowment for the Arts and the Mississippi Arts Commission and is part of the arts council’s Arts Incubator program, which supports creative small businesses in North Mississippi.

The event is free and open to the public, though attendees are encouraged to register in advance.

In addition to the workshop, Oxford-Lafayette Inc. is also accepting applications for the 2026 Oxford Pitch Competition , scheduled for June 11 at the Oxford Conference Center.

The competition, held in partnership with Innovate Mississippi and the Mississippi Small Business Development Center Network, offers entrepreneurs the chance to compete for cash prizes, gain exposure and receive one-on-one business coaching.

Applications are open through May 13.

The event will feature two tracks: one for traditional small businesses and another for high-growth startups with scalable, technology-driven models. Selected finalists will present their ideas during the competition, while all applicants will be connected with business development resources.

Organizers said the competition also serves as a qualifying event for Innovate Mississippi’s CoBuilders Accelerator, a 12-week program designed to help startups grow.

Both the workshop and pitch competition are intended to support entrepreneurs at various stages of development, from refining business strategies to securing funding and expanding operations.
